newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Hong Kong oil product sales can dip after handover.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong oil product sales can dip after handover.

text.p: Hong Kong oil terminal operators could suffer a drop in sales after the British colony reverts to Chinese rule at the end of June as Beijing is likely to clamp down on smuggling, industry sources said on Tuesday.

Terminal operators said they did not expect any change to existing tax or equity laws but conceded that the presence of Chinese police and custom officers in Hong Kong could be too much for the smugglers to cope with.
"I think the smugglers will look elsewhere. It's too close to home," one source said.
The terminal operators usually sell these cargoes on a free-on-board (fob) basis to barge operators who buy in 1,000 to 5,000-tonne lots, they said.

As the cargoes are sold on an fob basis, the terminal operators do not know their final destinations or whether the buyers have the proper documents or pay customs duties if the cargoes are taken into southern China.

Five major oil companies have terminals in Hong Kong and each can store between 200,000 and 350,000 cubic metres of oil products, sold for refuelling ships or to the local market as well as to barges.
The companies are Royal Dutch/Shell Group, Exxon Corp, Mobil Corp Caltex, a joint venture between Chevron Corp and Texaco Inc, and China Resources Co.
But the sources said that even after the handover, smuggling would not be totally eradicated.
"The terminals at the special zones are still used," one source said, referring to special economic zones set up by China to encourage industry.
He said in such zones, the smuggling could take the form of declaring less fuel to customs than is actually aboard or declaring a lower grade of fuel subject to less tax.

But traders said smugglers were already looking for alternative sources to Hong Kong in the Philippines and Okinawa. One independent terminal in the Philippines, operated by Subic Bay Petroleum Product Ltd, is reporting better sales as some of the larger barge operators have made trial purchases from there, they said.

Subic Bay Petroleum operates a 350,000-cubic metre storage terminal. A source close to the company said only 40 percent of the space is being used, but it expected demand to improve during the second half of the year with better planning of its sales outlets.

Industry sources said Hong Kong remained the best base for illegal trade as it takes at most one day to ship fuel to the furthest point in southern China, while its takes three days from the Philippines.
